title: Mao Zedong
subtitle: The founder of modern China, and the famine he caused

package.intro: Mao Zedong founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled it until his death in 1976. His Great Leap Forward caused the deadliest famine in recorded history, and his Cultural Revolution tore the country apart. This documentary tells his story, why many revile him, and why his portrait still hangs over Tiananmen Square.
facts: Born 26 December 1893 in Shaoshan, Hunan province
A delegate at the first congress of the Chinese Communist Party in Shanghai, July 1921
Fewer than 10,000 of the roughly 86,000 who began the Long March in 1934 reached the northwest
Proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949
More than 550,000 people were labelled 'rightists' in the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign
The Great Leap Forward (from 1958) led to a famine with estimated deaths of 15–45 million
Launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966; it ended with his death in 1976
Died in Beijing on 9 September 1976; a 1981 party resolution condemned the Cultural Revolution but upheld his overall record
package.sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Jonathan Spence's Mao Zedong, Philip Short's Mao: A Life, Yang Jisheng's Tombstone, Frank Dikötter's Mao's Great Famine, Roderick MacFarquhar and Michael Schoenhals's Mao's Last Revolution, the 1981 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: MAO ZEDONG
lines.sub: The founder of modern China, and the famine he caused

lines: On the first of October 1949, a tall man from Hunan stood on the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing and proclaimed the People's Republic of China.
After decades of civil war and invasion, nearly a quarter of humanity had a single ruler. Mao Zedong would lead China for the next twenty-seven years.

lines.label: estimated deaths in the famine of 1959 – 1961

lines: In that time, his Great Leap Forward caused the deadliest famine in recorded history, killing tens of millions of people.
Yet his portrait still hangs over Tiananmen Square, his face is on China's banknotes, and his embalmed body lies in a mausoleum visited by millions.
To the Chinese state, he is the founding father. To many historians and survivors, he was one of the most destructive rulers of the twentieth century. This is the story of both.

sections.name: A farmer's son
lines: Mao was born on the twenty-sixth of December 1893, in the village of Shaoshan, in Hunan province. His father was a strict farmer who had made himself prosperous.

lines.name: Mao Zedong
lines.role: A farmer's son from Hunan. Trained as a teacher.

lines: Mao clashed with his father and left home to study. He trained as a teacher in the provincial capital, Changsha, and read everything he could find.
In 1918 he worked as a library assistant at Peking University, at a time when young Chinese were angry at their country's weakness and searching for new ideas.
He found his answer in Marxism. In July 1921, he was one of the delegates at the founding congress of the Chinese Communist Party, in Shanghai.

lines.text: A revolution is not a dinner party.
lines.who: Mao Zedong, Report on the Peasant Movement in Hunan, 1927

lines: Most communists looked to factory workers. Mao believed revolution would come from China's vast peasantry. In 1927 he wrote that a revolution is not a dinner party.

sections.name: Civil war
lines: That year, the Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek turned on his communist allies and had thousands killed in Shanghai. A civil war began that would last, on and off, for twenty-two years.
Mao built a guerrilla army and a small communist state in the hills of Jiangxi. In purges there, thousands of suspected traitors in his own ranks were tortured and killed.
In 1934, surrounded by Nationalist armies, the communists broke out. The Long March took about a year and covered thousands of kilometres of mountains, rivers and marshland.

lines.label: of the main Red Army force that left Jiangxi reached the northwest

lines: Of the roughly eighty-six thousand who set out, fewer than ten thousand arrived. On the way, Mao became the movement's dominant leader.
In 1937, Japan launched a full-scale invasion of China. Communists and Nationalists formed an uneasy alliance, while Mao built up his strength at his base in Yan'an.
After Japan surrendered, the civil war resumed. The Nationalists, corrupt and exhausted, collapsed, and in 1949 Chiang fled to the island of Taiwan.

sections.name: The new China
lines: The new government brought real change. A marriage law in 1950 banned arranged marriages and gave women the right to divorce. Campaigns spread literacy and basic healthcare.
Land was taken from landlords and handed to peasants. But it was done through mass 'struggle sessions', in which villagers were urged to denounce and attack landlords.
Historians estimate that at least one to two million people were killed in land reform. Hundreds of thousands more were executed as counter-revolutionaries.
In 1956, Mao invited intellectuals to criticise the party: let a hundred flowers bloom. The criticism that came was fierce.
He struck back. In the Anti-Rightist Campaign of 1957, more than half a million people were branded rightists. Many were sent to labour camps or lost their careers for decades.

sections.name: The Great Leap
lines: In 1958 Mao launched the Great Leap Forward, to overtake Britain in steel production within fifteen years. Peasants were organised into huge communes and ate in communal canteens.
Tens of millions were pulled off the land to make steel in backyard furnaces. Pots, tools and doors were melted down. Much of the metal was useless.
Local officials, afraid of being called rightists, reported impossible harvests. The state took grain based on those false figures, leaving villages with almost nothing.

lines.name: Peng Dehuai
lines.role: Defence minister. Warned Mao in 1959 that something was wrong.

lines: In 1959, at a party meeting at Lushan, the defence minister, Peng Dehuai, privately warned Mao that the policy was failing. Mao denounced and purged him. Officials learned to stay silent.
The result was the deadliest famine in recorded history. Grain exports continued, and in many places people trying to flee in search of food were stopped by militia.
Estimates of the deaths range from about fifteen million to more than forty-five million. Many demographers put the figure at around thirty million.
Mao stepped back from day-to-day government, and other leaders, among them Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, quietly reversed his policies. Mao came to see them as a threat.

sections.name: The Cultural Revolution
lines: In 1966 he launched the Cultural Revolution, calling on the young to rebel against the party establishment. Millions of students formed Red Guard units and rallied in Tiananmen Square.

lines.label: copies of the 'Little Red Book' printed

lines: His sayings were collected in the Little Red Book, printed in more than a billion copies. His image was everywhere.

Teachers, officials, writers and anyone with the wrong family background were humiliated and beaten at public meetings. Many were killed or took their own lives. Temples, books and artworks were destroyed.
Liu Shaoqi, the head of state, was expelled from the party and died in custody in 1969, denied proper medical care. Deng Xiaoping was purged and sent to work in a tractor factory.
When the Red Guards descended into factional fighting, Mao turned to the army to restore order, and around seventeen million young people were sent to live and work in the countryside.
Most estimates of the deaths in the Cultural Revolution range from several hundred thousand to around two million.
Abroad, Mao made a surprising turn. In February 1972, the American president, Richard Nixon, came to Beijing to meet him.

sections.name: The end

lines.name: Chairman Mao
lines.role: Chairman of the Communist Party until his death.

lines: By then Mao was old and ill. He died in Beijing on the ninth of September 1976, aged eighty-two.

lines.label: Trial of the Gang of Four · 1980 – 1981

lines: Within a month, his widow, Jiang Qing, and three allies, the so-called Gang of Four, were arrested. They were later put on trial and blamed for the worst of the Cultural Revolution.

In 1981, the party under Deng Xiaoping gave its verdict. It condemned the Cultural Revolution, but ruled that Mao's achievements outweighed his mistakes. The verdict is often summed up as seventy percent right, thirty percent wrong.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: Mao's defenders point to a China unified and independent after a century of foreign humiliation, to legal equality for women, and to life expectancy that rose from around thirty-five years to over sixty.

Critics answer that no achievement required tens of millions of deaths. Inside China, those deaths remain a sensitive subject. The journalist Yang Jisheng's history of the famine, Tombstone, is banned there.

lines.text: The portrait and the graves are one story.

lines: Mao's face still looks out over Tiananmen Square. The graves of the famine lie in the countryside, many of them unmarked.
Both belong to the same man. China honours the first. Its people are still not free to remember the second in full.
